nameStory: The winter polypore earned its name by being one of the few fungi brave enough to fruit during New England's coldest months. While most mushrooms call it quits after the first frost, this hardy species keeps appearing on dead branches throughout winter, giving mushroom hunters something to discover even in snowy woods.
description: Winter polypore is a small, bracket-like fungus that grows on dead hardwood branches and logs. It typically measures 1-4 inches across with a brownish, fan-shaped cap that has a leathery texture. Unlike many bracket fungi, it has a distinct stem that connects it to the wood, making it look more like a traditional mushroom than a shelf fungus. The underside features tiny pores instead of gills, which is where it releases its spores.

idTips.label: Seasonality
idTips.description: Fruits primarily in winter when most other fungi are dormant, persisting through cold weather and even light snow cover

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Fan-shaped and brownish, with a tough, leathery texture that feels dry and somewhat flexible when fresh

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Underside has tiny white to cream-colored pores that may appear slightly yellowed with age, no gills present

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Has a distinct lateral stem that attaches to dead wood, unlike many bracket fungi that attach directly to the substrate

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always found on dead hardwood branches and logs, particularly oak, maple, and birch, causing white rot decay

idTips.label: Safety
idTips.description: Inedible due to tough, leathery texture - never eat any wild mushroom without expert identification

habitat: Look for winter polypore on dead branches and fallen logs of hardwood trees throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. It's particularly common on oak, maple, and birch wood, often appearing on branches that are still attached to trees but have died. You'll find it from sea level to mountain elevations, anywhere hardwood trees grow.

seasonality.spring: May still be visible from winter fruiting, but new growth is uncommon. Old specimens become weathered and fade to grayish colors.
seasonality.summer: Rarely fruits during warm months. Any specimens found are likely old and dried out from winter, appearing brittle and discolored.
seasonality.fall: Begins to appear in late fall as temperatures drop and other fungi disappear. Early specimens are fresh and show the best color and texture.
seasonality.winter: Peak season for fresh specimens. Actively fruits during cold months, appearing on snow-covered logs and maintaining its form despite freezing temperatures.

funFact: Winter polypore has a built-in antifreeze system that allows it to keep growing and releasing spores even when temperatures drop below freezing, making it one of nature's most cold-hardy mushrooms.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small bracket fungi, but the winter fruiting season and presence of a distinct stem help distinguish it. Remember: if you're finding fresh bracket fungi in January, you're likely looking at winter polypore.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a polypore (meaning 'many pores'), this species was recently moved between different fungal families as DNA studies revealed new relationships. The name 'Lentinus' comes from the Latin word for 'flexible,' referring to the bendable nature of fungi in this genus.
compareHints: Winter polypore differs from its relatives Tiger Sawgill and Spring Polypore primarily in its fruiting season and coloration. Tiger Sawgill has distinctive dark scales and fruits in warmer months, while Spring Polypore appears in spring with a more circular cap shape. Winter polypore is the only one in its genus that consistently fruits during cold weather.
